The order of iterators matters — a filter and a map is not the same as a map and a filter!

You might wonder why the first filter uses `*x` and the second filter does not. 
`v.iter()` produces an `Iterator<Item = &i32>`. The `.filter()` call takes an `Iterator<Item = T>` as input,
and passes `&T` to its predicate. Therefore `x: &&i32` on line 3. The Rust standard library implements the
remainder operator `%` for `&i32` on the left-hand side ([see the docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.Rem.html#impl-Rem%3Ci32%3E-for-%26'a+i32)),
but not for `&&i32`. So we have to dereference `x` once to use it in the expression `*x % 2`.

By contrast on line 4, when `.map()` takes an `Iterator<Item = T>` as input, it passes `T` to its closure.
Therefore the closure in `map` takes `&i32` as input. The multiplication operator `*` is implemented for `&i32`,
so `x` does not need to be dereferenced in `x * 2`. The operation `x * 2` produces a value of type `i32`, so
the result of the map is an `Iterator<Item = i32>`. The `filter` then takes `x : &i32`, which also does not need
a dereference to do `x % 2`. Now you know!

do you need to wrap `T` in a newtype?
answer: `Trait` is defined in an external crate and `T` is defined in an external crate
distractors: `Trait` is defined in the local crate and `T` is defined in an external crate
`Trait` is defined in an external crate and `T` is defined in the local crate
`Trait` is defined in the local crate and `T` is defined in the local crate
questions.context:
The orphan rule dictates that a trait cannot be implemented for a type if both are
defined in an external crate, thus necessitating a newtype. If either the trait or the type
are defined locally, then a newtype is unnecessary.

questions.prompt:
Which of the following are valid reasons for implementing a macro as a
procedural macro instead of a declarative macro?
answer: You want to integrate with Rust's derive system
Your macro requires nontrivial analysis of the macro user's syntax
distractors: You want to generate variable-length sequences of code
Your macro requires an entire item as input, not just an expression
questions.context:
Procedural macros are the only way to create a custom derive. Procedural macros
are also useful when you need code to analyze the macro user's syntax — declarative
macros only permit shuffling around the input, not e.g. computing its size.

Declarative macros can generate variable-length sequences of code, and can wrap/produce
items and not just expressions.

questions.prompt: Which of the following best describes the input to a procedural macro?
answer: The input is a sequence of tokens
distractors: The input is a typed control-flow graph
The input is an abstract syntax tree
The input is a byte-string
questions.context:
Procedural macros take as input (and produce as output) token streams.
You can use crates like `syn` to convert tokens to syntax trees.
